references.appraisal: Actual 260-page official PDF retained from Phase 7. Introductory recognition and supervised referral boundaries only, not qualification for child casework, family mediation, clinical care or a Nigerian mandatory-reporting/legal-age decision.

Seven strategy domains are programme guidance, not proof that a short local awareness event reduces violence. Evidence and contextual adaptation still require critical review.

references.author: Leight J and colleagues
references.title: Effectiveness of community mobilisation and group-based interventions for preventing intimate partner violence against women in low- and middle-income countries: A systematic review and meta-analysis
references.use: Interpret prevention evidence without transferring a pooled estimate or programme design directly to a new setting.
references.appraisal: Primary publisher indexed methods/results/limitations read; direct PDF download returned a restriction page, not an archived PDF. Search to 20 July 2021; 30 studies of 27 unique RCTs, substantial heterogeneity (I-squared 83%), English-only studies and self-report/selection limitations. Odds are not risks; neither a promised local effect nor a synthesis of attitude/norm outcomes is justified.

courses.title: Community Prevention and Social Norms Change
courses.school_name: School of Gender Studies and Gender-Based Violence Prevention
courses.audience: Introductory social work and community-service learners using non-graphic fictional scenarios. No specialist child/GBV casework, clinical, forensic, legal or research competence is conferred; supervised skills and safeguarding review are separate requirements.
courses.study_guidance: Use only the supplied non-graphic fictional scenarios and aggregate exercise data. Do not seek real disclosures, investigate allegations or submit survivor records, passwords or images. Write your reasoning before checking feedback. You may pause or use an alternative fictional exercise; supervised skills review remains separate.
courses.practice_safety_note: Use only the supplied non-graphic fictional scenario or aggregate exercise data. Do not collect real disclosures or submit survivor records, passwords or images. You may pause or use an alternative fictional exercise. Record reasoning before checking guide feedback.
courses.outcome: Prepare a bounded fictional prevention plan that distinguishes attitudes, social expectations and behaviour, protects participation and uses appropriately limited evidence to review outcomes.

modules.title: Attitudes expectations and reference groups
modules.outcome: Distinguish personal attitudes from perceived social expectations and identify a testable prevention assumption.
paragraphs: An individual attitude concerns what someone personally considers acceptable. A social expectation concerns what someone believes relevant other people do or approve of, including the consequences expected for disagreeing. These can differ: a person may privately reject an unequal rule but expect exclusion if they challenge it. In a fictional discussion, identify the behaviour, the people whose approval matters and the possible social consequence. Do not assume that every participant shares a belief, or infer a community norm from one confident speaker. A proposed explanation remains an assumption until appropriately examined. [S16, S1]

Prevention addresses conditions that enable violence, while an immediate support response addresses the needs and choices of a person affected. Both require resources and responsible roles. A community event does not replace a confidential referral pathway, and a disclosure should never be sought to make a prevention session convincing. The inter-agency standards provide a quality benchmark for participation and services. Respectful discussion should challenge coercion without identifying a family, treating a community as inherently violent or asking people to defend their private experiences before others. [S10, S1]

The RESPECT framework connects several prevention strategies rather than describing one universal campaign. Its updated edition can help a planner consider how relationships, service access, economic conditions, environments and expectations interact. For this introductory exercise, select a narrow change that a service or group can influence and state why that change might matter. A theory of change links an activity to a plausible mechanism, an intermediate change and an intended outcome. Drawing arrows between them is a reasoned proposal, not proof that the mechanism operates locally or that the outcome will follow. [S16, R25]

Research on community and group interventions includes trials with differing contexts, designs and durations. The 2023 meta-analysis searched through July 2021 and found substantial variation across trials. Its pooled odds estimate cannot be promised to a new community, converted casually into a risk reduction or used to validate every activity labelled gender transformative. For a fictional plan, state the relevant research type, the period it covers and one transfer limitation. Treat a participant's agreement during a session as a learning observation, not as evidence that behaviour or violence has changed. [R24, R25]
modules.example: Fictional case: a youth club privately questions a rule excluding women from budget decisions, but members expect criticism from senior peers if they disagree publicly. The learner distinguishes private views, perceived approval and the club's actual decision rule without asking for violence histories.
modules.activity: Write four lines: the behaviour, a private-attitude question, a perceived-expectation question and a provisional mechanism for a feasible club-rule review. Identify one evidence gap and one claim the exercise cannot support.
modules.feedback: A useful analysis separates attitudes, perceived expectations and observed behaviour. It identifies relevant others without assuming consensus and keeps a plausible mechanism distinct from demonstrated prevention.

modules.title: Co-design delivery and safe participation
modules.outcome: Specify a feasible prevention activity with participation, support and delivery safeguards.
paragraphs: Co-design means affected people can influence a relevant decision, with an honest explanation of what is open to change. Invite different perspectives through appropriate accessible routes rather than rely only on officials or digitally connected participants. Consider language, disability access, timing, childcare and transport as practical design questions. Participation should not require someone to identify as a survivor, describe an incident or publicly contradict a person who controls their access to resources. Use original fictional discussion material in this course; real consultation requires approved specialist arrangements and appropriate confidentiality. [S10, S1]

A narrow plan should identify its intended participants, the specific behaviour or institutional rule to address and the responsible decision-maker. Compare feasible activities with the proposed mechanism instead of selecting a slogan first. A repeated facilitated discussion might help examine expectations, while changing a registration rule requires the role authorised to change it. Neither should be represented as universally sufficient. The review of reviews organises prevention evidence across strategy areas, but the underlying reviews vary in quality and evidence period. A strategy heading does not establish that a particular local activity is effective. [R25, S16]

Delivery conditions include trained facilitation, accessible materials, safeguarding oversight, confidential support options and a plan for adverse reactions. Agree how a facilitator will pause a discussion that becomes identifying or coercive, and who will handle a voluntary request for help outside the public session. Do not promise complete confidentiality in a group, assume a referral service has capacity or direct learners to mediate a violent relationship. Check the current scope, eligibility, contact arrangements and responsible specialist role through authorised organisational channels before including a service in an actual delivery plan. [S10, S1]

A plan also needs time, operating resources, accepted responsibilities and a review point. Longer or more complex programmes cannot be reduced to a single event without reconsidering their mechanism and evidence. Budget labels should not conceal unpaid burdens on participants or frontline workers. State what cannot proceed until a dependency is met, such as accessible communication or specialist support availability. In a fictional proposal, recommend a limited pilot and a decision rule for revision rather than promise immediate scale. A safe route for disagreement and feedback belongs in the delivery design from the beginning. [S16, R24, S10]
modules.example: Fictional case: a club can review its speaking and budget rules but has no private support route and schedules every meeting during market work. A proposed launch is paused while the responsible organiser checks access arrangements and qualified support capacity.
modules.activity: Draft a delivery note naming the decision participants can influence, two access adjustments, a facilitator boundary, a verified-support dependency, an owner and a review point. Explain why an unresolved dependency changes the launch decision.
modules.feedback: A coherent note connects the activity to its mechanism and authority. It makes access and support dependencies explicit, avoids forced disclosure and does not mistake a proposed referral or unresourced promise for readiness.

modules.title: Review outcomes harms and adaptation
modules.outcome: Separate outputs, intermediate changes and violence outcomes in a bounded review plan.
paragraphs: An output records what was delivered, such as sessions held or materials supplied. An intermediate change might concern an understood rule, a perceived expectation or an opportunity to participate. A violence outcome concerns experiences or behaviour over a defined period and requires substantially different ethical and methodological arrangements. Do not treat attendance, favourable feedback or an intention stated in a workshop as proof that violence declined. A fictional learning exercise can assess the quality of a proposed review without collecting survivor information, administering a sensitive survey or attempting to calculate community prevalence. [S16, S10]

Write a review question before selecting a measure. For a club-rule pilot, a reasonable question might concern whether intended participants could influence a specific decision under the revised procedure. Define the period, who is included, the data source and the limits of the claim. Where views differ, retain the disagreement rather than average away an access concern. Anonymous feedback can still be identifying in a small setting. Any real-world collection involving GBV needs specialist ethical and safety arrangements; a course worksheet, verbal permission from a leader or a desire for evidence is not sufficient authorisation. [S10, S1]

Prevention evidence should be appraised for both findings and fit. The trial synthesis examines IPV outcomes but did not meta-analyse attitudes or social norms as separate non-IPV outcomes. The review of reviews searches through April 2022 despite its later publication. Publication year therefore does not equal the last date of included evidence. Neither review removes the need to examine local delivery, who was reached, missing perspectives, alternative explanations and possible adverse effects. A change observed after a programme can be important without establishing that the programme caused it. [R24, R25]

A useful review leads to an accountable decision: continue within scope, revise, pause or seek further specialist assessment. Assign a responsible role and a realistic review date. Examine whether an activity increased burden, conflict or exclusion, and do not blame participants when a design assumption fails. Share only an appropriately limited summary through approved arrangements. Preserve the difference between a defensible recommendation and a claim of proven transformation. A short course develops evidence-aware planning; approving a curriculum, implementing a prevention programme and demonstrating a reduction in violence remain separate tasks. [S16, S10, S1]
modules.example: Fictional case: a club runs three discussions and reports better understanding of a rule. Its report says violence was reduced, although it measured no violence outcome. A learner corrects the claim and proposes an accessible decision-participation review with an accountable owner.
modules.activity: Prepare an output, an intermediate-change question, an unsupported claim to remove, an adverse-effect check and an action owner. State why a before/after observation alone cannot establish causation.
modules.feedback: Sessions and reported understanding are relevant observations, with limited claims. A defensible review separates outcome levels, examines access and possible harms, recognises alternative explanations and assigns a response.

assessment.title: Community Prevention and Social Norms Change

modules.title: Attitudes expectations and reference groups
modules.outcome: Distinguish personal attitudes from perceived social expectations and identify a testable prevention assumption.

teaching_points.text: Private attitudes and perceived social expectations can differ.
A reference group is identified contextually.
Prevention sessions should not solicit survivor testimony.
A theory of change states a mechanism that still needs evidence.
Pooled prevention findings do not guarantee a local reduction.

modules.title: Co-design delivery and safe participation
modules.outcome: Specify a feasible prevention activity with participation, support and delivery safeguards.

teaching_points.text: Co-design requires meaningful decision influence.
Access conditions belong in delivery planning.
A proposed referral is not verified service capacity.
Facilitation needs a boundary for identifying discussion.
Unmet dependencies affect readiness.

modules.title: Review outcomes harms and adaptation
modules.outcome: Separate outputs, intermediate changes and violence outcomes in a bounded review plan.

teaching_points.text: Delivery outputs are distinct from violence outcomes.
A review measure follows its question.
Evidence search dates differ from publication dates.
A before/after difference does not alone establish causation.
A review should support an accountable response.

questions.question: A club member rejects exclusion privately but expects peer criticism for opposing it. Which distinction matters?

options.text: Private disagreement proves that no social pressure exists.
One member's account establishes everyone's belief.
Personal attitude differs from perceived social approval.
Perceived approval and observed behaviour are identical.

questions.rationale: The account concerns both a personal view and an expectation about others.

questions.question: For a fictional budget-rule discussion, how should a learner identify whose approval matters?

options.text: Assume the loudest speaker represents all residents.
Choose a reference group solely from a national stereotype.
Treat all social contacts as equally influential by definition.
Ask which people are relevant to that specific decision and retain uncertainty.

questions.rationale: Influence depends on the particular behaviour and context.

questions.question: A facilitator wants personal disclosures to make a norms workshop persuasive. What fits the course?

options.text: Use fictional discussion and maintain an appropriate confidential support pathway.
Require participants to disclose for attendance credit.
Invite the group to investigate a named family.
Replace referral capacity with a public testimony contest.

questions.rationale: Participation need not expose private histories to support prevention learning.

questions.question: An activity-to-outcome diagram has been drafted. What does it establish at this point?

options.text: Causal effectiveness because the arrows are clear.
A proposed explanation to examine, rather than proof of local effect.
A guarantee that all intermediate changes occurred.
Permission to omit implementation and outcome checks.

questions.rationale: A causal proposal is not a completed evaluation.

questions.question: A planner cites heterogeneous trials to promise an identical result after one local meeting. What correction is needed?

options.text: Treat pooled odds as an identical absolute risk change everywhere.
Assume any meeting matches every studied programme.
Consider context, intervention content, duration and evidence limits before making a local claim.
Present participant agreement as proof that violence stopped.

questions.rationale: The research supports careful design and appraisal rather than an automatic transferred effect.

questions.question: Participants are invited after all programme decisions are fixed. What should the organiser clarify?

options.text: That attendance alone proves shared decision-making.
That consultation requires disclosure of abuse.
That only officials can identify participation barriers.
Which decisions can still change and how participant input will affect them.

questions.rationale: Participation needs an honest scope of influence.

questions.question: A fictional prevention meeting excludes traders through its timing. What is a relevant adjustment?

options.text: Review timing with intended participants and assess practical access needs.
Assume absence means agreement with harmful norms.
Publish names of those who cannot attend.
Ignore timing because the presentation is well designed.

questions.rationale: Access barriers affect who can contribute and should inform design.

questions.question: A programme lists a support number copied from an old flyer. What remains necessary before actual use?

options.text: A guarantee based only on the flyer logo.
Authorised confirmation of current scope, eligibility and safe contact arrangements.
A learner test call disclosing a real person's history.
An assumption that all services can accept every referral.

questions.rationale: A usable support pathway needs current, appropriate verification.

questions.question: A group begins naming a household while discussing a fictional scenario. What should the facilitator do?

options.text: Ask the group to investigate the household.
Record the allegations for the course worksheet.
Pause the identifying discussion and use the agreed safeguarding and private-support arrangements.
Turn the named account into public campaign content.

questions.rationale: The activity should not expose or investigate real people.

questions.question: Accessible materials and qualified support remain unconfirmed. How should a plan describe launch status?

options.text: Ready because the poster has been printed.
Ready if participants sign away all risks.
Ready because future funding is possible.
Conditional on resolving those dependencies through assigned responsible roles.

questions.rationale: Delivery readiness requires resources and accepted responsibilities beyond outputs.

questions.question: A report records three sessions and calls them proof of reduced violence. What is justified?

options.text: The sessions are an output; a violence-reduction claim needs appropriate separate evidence.
Every session is a measured violence outcome.
Attendance proves every participant changed behaviour.
A polished report establishes causal impact.

questions.rationale: The recorded measure supports a delivery claim, not the stated violence outcome.

questions.question: A pilot aims to improve influence over club decisions. Which review is most relevant within approved arrangements?

options.text: Only the number of presentation slides.
Whether intended participants could influence the specified decision, with period and coverage stated.
The facilitator's assumption that silence means agreement.
Unrelated incident details collected by learners.

questions.rationale: The measure should address the intended change and remain within ethical scope.

questions.question: A 2025 review searches through April 2022. How should its currency be described?

options.text: All included evidence was collected in 2025.
The search automatically includes 2026 studies.
Published in 2025, with included searches ending in April 2022.
A publication date removes the need to examine the search period.

questions.rationale: Both dates matter when assessing currency.

questions.question: A club records improved understanding after a pilot without a comparison design. What remains possible?

options.text: The programme is necessarily the only cause.
Every missing participant improved by the same amount.
No further appraisal can be useful.
Other explanations, differences in participation and reporting effects may contribute.

questions.rationale: An observed change needs interpretation consistent with the design.

questions.question: Feedback suggests a fictional activity increased exclusion. What should follow?

options.text: An assigned review of the concern and a justified revision or pause with feedback.
Blame absent participants and close the review.
Publish identifying details to defend the activity.
Continue unchanged because materials were already produced.

questions.rationale: Programme accountability includes responding to possible harms and design failure.

courses.title: Child Marriage FGM and Harmful Practices
courses.cover_title:
Child Marriage FGM
and Harmful Practices
courses.school_name: School of Gender Studies and Gender-Based Violence Prevention
courses.audience: Introductory social work and community-service learners using non-graphic fictional scenarios. No specialist child/GBV casework, clinical, forensic, legal or research competence is conferred; supervised skills and safeguarding review are separate requirements.
courses.study_guidance: Use only the supplied non-graphic fictional scenarios and aggregate exercise data. Do not seek real disclosures, investigate allegations or submit survivor records, passwords or images. Write your reasoning before checking feedback. You may pause or use an alternative fictional exercise; supervised skills review remains separate.
courses.practice_safety_note: Use only the supplied non-graphic fictional scenario or aggregate exercise data. Do not collect real disclosures or submit survivor records, passwords or images. You may pause or use an alternative fictional exercise. Record reasoning before checking guide feedback.
courses.outcome: Analyse non-graphic fictional harmful-practice concerns through rights, best interests and qualified safeguarding, distinguishing prevention evidence from clinical or legal competence.

modules.title: Rights context and respectful recognition
modules.outcome: Recognise harmful-practice concerns without stereotyping, investigation or unsupported legal conclusions.
paragraphs: Child marriage and female genital mutilation raise distinct protection, health and rights concerns. They should not be collapsed into one experience or treated as an inevitable characteristic of any community. Discuss the reported concern, the person's access to support and the appropriate qualified role rather than infer practices from ethnicity, religion, nationality or appearance. A respectful response can challenge harm while recognising the person as a rights-holder with priorities and strengths. This course uses non-graphic fictional scenarios and does not ask learners to identify affected classmates, inspect bodies or investigate families. [S1, S10, S14]

Social and economic pressures may shape the choices available to girls and families, but a contextual explanation does not excuse harm. Community leaders' views are not substitutes for an individual child's welfare or meaningful participation. The updated child-marriage chapter addresses girls at risk and girls who are already married, separated, divorced or widowed. Support must not disappear because a prevention opportunity has passed. Educational, psychosocial, protection and qualified health needs can remain relevant, with a coordinated response appropriate to the person's circumstances rather than a single label or public campaign category. [S11, S10]

Recognition is different from establishing facts, making a diagnosis or determining legal status. An introductory learner should not decide whether a particular marriage is valid, issue a universal statement about Nigerian reporting duties or infer an imminent threat from a demographic characteristic. Applicable jurisdiction, organisational safeguarding procedures and qualified advice matter. If an actual concern arises, follow authorised safeguarding and emergency arrangements appropriate to the setting rather than use a course exercise as a decision protocol. Avoid promising absolute secrecy, confronting a suspected actor or arranging informal family mediation. [S11, S1]

The 2025 WHO overview expands guidance on FGM prevention and care, including education and health-worker capacity. Reading its overview does not qualify a learner to examine, classify or treat FGM. Qualified care should be accessible without stigma, and involvement by a health worker does not make a harmful practice acceptable. A fictional support note can identify a need for appropriate clinical expertise while excluding anatomical details, procedural advice and medical claims. Keep the person's dignity, privacy and practical access needs visible; never make coursework depend on graphic description or personal testimony. [S14, S10, S1]
modules.example: Fictional case: a youth service hears a non-graphic concern about a girl leaving school for marriage. A learner recognises a safeguarding concern and the need for qualified advice, without deciding legal status, contacting the family or naming the girl in class.
modules.activity: Write a recognition note stating the concern, two rights/access questions, an uncertainty, the appropriate specialist role and three actions outside this learner's scope. Use no identifying or graphic details.
modules.feedback: A sound note challenges harm without stereotyping. It distinguishes concern from proof, preserves dignity and routes child protection, legal and health questions through qualified procedures rather than personal investigation.

modules.title: Best interests assent and safe support
modules.outcome: Identify child-specific communication and safeguarding needs without applying an adult consent shortcut.
paragraphs: A child's best interests require careful attention to safety, wellbeing, rights and the likely effects of proposed actions. They are not simply an adult's preference or a convenient reason to ignore the child's views. The updated child-marriage chapter emphasises evolving capacities and age-appropriate communication. Qualified staff should help a child understand relevant options in ways suited to development, language and disability needs. In this introductory exercise, describe why a specialist process is needed and what uncertainties should be communicated; do not attempt a capacity assessment, a best-interests determination or a real case interview. [S11, S1]

Consent and assent are related but distinct. A child's affirmative participation is not automatically equivalent to an adult's legal authorisation, and a guardian's involvement is not automatically safe or sufficient for every action. Qualified procedures must consider applicable law, decision-specific capacity, safe caregiver involvement, the child's views and potential conflicts of interest. The course does not supply a universal age table or reporting rule. Do not assume the accompanying adult should receive a disclosure, or that a form signed by any adult resolves confidentiality and safeguarding concerns. [S11, S10]

A child may not use the language of abuse or may describe mixed feelings about a proposed marriage. Respectful listening does not require the child to adopt a label before accessing appropriate support. Avoid repeated questioning, promises about outcomes and pressure to provide proof. A learner should not contact a family, broker an agreement or direct the child to confront someone. Actual concerns need the designated qualified safeguarding process, with urgent needs handled through authorised arrangements. Explain foreseeable limits to privacy honestly through appropriate communication rather than promise that information can never be shared. [S11, S1]

A bounded handover identifies the concern and the responsible qualified role, using only necessary information through an approved channel. Do not place names, locations, incident narratives or images in course submissions. In a fictional plan, show how communication access, a safe contact route and follow-up responsibility would be considered by authorised staff. Where information is missing, retain uncertainty instead of resolving it by assumption. Specialist supervision matters because well-intended actions, including an unplanned family conversation or an unsafe contact attempt, may increase risk. The exercise assesses reasoning about boundaries, not readiness for independent child casework. [S11, S10]
modules.example: Fictional case: an adolescent asks a youth-service worker about continuing school and says the adult accompanying her should not hear the conversation. The learner identifies child-specific safeguarding and communication questions without assuming the adult is a safe guardian or promising an outcome.
modules.activity: Draft a supervised support outline: child participation, consent/assent distinction, caregiver uncertainty, privacy limits, a qualified decision route and safe follow-up responsibility. Explain why an adult-only consent approach is inadequate.
modules.feedback: A defensible outline considers best interests and evolving capacities without replacing specialist decisions. It does not equate assent with legal consent, assume caregiver safety or initiate a family intervention.

modules.title: Prevention evidence and coordinated access
modules.outcome: Appraise FGM education evidence and propose a bounded support/prevention review.
paragraphs: Prevention of harmful practices needs respectful engagement, meaningful participation and links to appropriate services. A public promise or awareness activity may be a useful process observation, but it does not establish that harm has ceased. Avoid framing community participation as a request to reveal affected individuals or demonstrate compliance through inspections. A fictional prevention proposal can identify an educational aim, responsible facilitator, access needs and safeguarding dependencies. Clinical, legal and specialist child-protection decisions belong to qualified roles, and a prevention organiser should not make service use conditional on public agreement with the campaign. [S10, S1, S14]

The 2026 review of education and FGM prevention includes four observational studies searched through May 2023. Its findings are rated very low certainty and concern knowledge, attitudes, reported commitment and requests for reinfibulation. These outcomes differ from measured incidence of FGM. Neither the later publication year nor Nigerian authorship converts the findings into proof that a particular Nigerian counselling approach prevents FGM. Describe education as an evidence-informed option requiring contextual design and evaluation; do not promise an effect, reproduce a source intervention or present the review title as proof of every counselling format. [R26, S14]

Coordinated access means the relevant qualified services understand their roles and the person can consider suitable support within appropriate safeguarding arrangements. A health need, school-access problem and child-protection concern may require different expertise and information permissions. Do not send a full narrative to every provider because several services might be useful. Check actual service scope and authorised communication, and keep unresolved access barriers visible. A learner's fictional outline can specify responsibilities and review questions; it cannot promise care availability, direct a treatment, decide mandatory reporting or certify that a referral has been completed. [S11, S10, S1]

A limited review should separate what was delivered, what participants understood and what remains unknown about behaviour and harm. Examine who could not participate and whether discussion created stigma, pressure or identifying information. Any real assessment involving children or sensitive GBV information needs appropriate specialist ethical and safeguarding arrangements. In this course, use only the supplied fictional cases to identify a defensible next decision, an evidence gap and an accountable owner. Course completion, a campaign pledge and an approved professional service are different achievements; none should be substituted for another in a programme report. [R26, S10, S1]
modules.example: Fictional case: an organiser reports that an educational meeting ended FGM because participants expressed disapproval. A learner retains the observed learning result, removes the unsupported incidence claim and adds qualified safeguarding, access and evidence-review requirements.
modules.activity: Prepare a prevention-review note with the observed outcome, its evidence limit, a potential participation harm, qualified support roles and a review owner. Explain why stated commitment is not a measured incidence reduction.
modules.feedback: A careful note uses the review's very low-certainty findings honestly. It supports respectful prevention and coordinated access without claiming clinical competence, legal authority or a demonstrated reduction in harm.

questions.question: An adult says a child's views are irrelevant because the adult knows best. What needs correction?

A child's participation has no place in safeguarding.
One adult statement settles every potential consequence.

That age-appropriate communication can be useful.
That qualified procedures remain necessary.
That the child's views should be heard respectfully.

questions.question: A youth-service worker is uncertain whether an accompanying adult is safe to involve. What is appropriate?

Use the designated qualified safeguarding process rather than assume disclosure is safe.
Invite the adult to mediate without review.

questions.question: A fictional girl discusses a proposed marriage without calling it violence. What response fits this course?

As limited evidence requiring contextual appraisal and cautious claims.
As proof that all included studies were Nigerian trials.

questions.question: Several providers may assist a fictional child. What should the support outline specify?

courses.title: Technology Facilitated Abuse and Digital Safety
courses.cover_title:
Technology Facilitated
Abuse and Digital Safety
courses.school_name: School of Gender Studies and Gender-Based Violence Prevention
courses.audience: Introductory social work and community-service learners using non-graphic fictional scenarios. No specialist child/GBV casework, clinical, forensic, legal or research competence is conferred; supervised skills and safeguarding review are separate requirements.
courses.study_guidance: Use only the supplied non-graphic fictional scenarios and aggregate exercise data. Do not seek real disclosures, investigate allegations or submit survivor records, passwords or images. Write your reasoning before checking feedback. You may pause or use an alternative fictional exercise; supervised skills review remains separate.
courses.practice_safety_note: Use only the supplied non-graphic fictional scenario or aggregate exercise data. Do not collect real disclosures or submit survivor records, passwords or images. You may pause or use an alternative fictional exercise. Record reasoning before checking guide feedback.
courses.outcome: Develop a fictional survivor-centred digital-support outline that recognises technology-related coercion, preserves choice and privacy and routes technical and legal questions to qualified roles.

modules.title: Digital abuse power and evidence
modules.outcome: Recognise technology-related control while distinguishing reports, research findings and technical verification.
paragraphs: Technology can be used to threaten, monitor, impersonate, exclude or distribute material without consent. Such behaviour can connect online spaces with offline control over relationships, income, movement or reputation. Ask about the behaviour and its effects on choice and access rather than assume online harm is less serious or entirely separate from a person's circumstances. Conversely, a troubling device symptom does not establish who caused it or whether surveillance occurred. An introductory learner should distinguish what a person reports from what has been technically verified, without requiring forensic proof before respectful support is offered. [S17, S1]

Gender, disability, language, age, sexuality and access to independent devices can affect how a person experiences harm and seeks assistance. Technology may also be essential for work, support networks or accessible communication. Telling someone simply to leave the internet can remove valuable resources and shift responsibility away from the person using abuse. A survivor-centred response asks what matters to the person and what forms of contact or assistance are feasible. It avoids treating a platform feature, device ownership or a demographic category as a complete explanation of the problem. [S17, S1]

The 2026 regional scoping review maps studies of technology-facilitated GBV in sub-Saharan Africa. It reports uneven geographic coverage and substantial attention to university and young populations. A map of reported forms and experiences does not estimate representative regional prevalence or prove that the same tactic affects everyone in the same way. The measurement scoping review also identifies gaps in what existing instruments capture. Neither article supplies a diagnostic test for a person's phone or validates a universal Nigerian checklist for deciding whether a reported experience is real. [R27, R28]

Generative AI can amplify impersonation and non-consensual fabricated content, but a learner should not authenticate an image, request intimate material or produce an abusive demonstration. Respond to the reported concern within the appropriate support role and route specialist technical or legal questions through approved arrangements. Course exercises contain descriptions only; do not upload passwords, private messages, identifying screenshots or sexual images. In particular, never solicit or circulate sexual material involving children. A non-graphic fictional account is enough to assess careful reasoning without creating further exposure or attempting a criminal investigation. [S17, S1]
modules.example: Fictional case: an adult reports threats involving a fabricated image and says her shared device is also needed for work. A learner recognises the access and coercion concerns without requesting the image, diagnosing spyware or instructing her to abandon the device.
modules.activity: Write a support-analysis note separating the reported behaviour, access consequence, technical uncertainty, person-led priority and appropriate qualified role. Name material that must not be requested for this coursework.
modules.feedback: A useful note takes the concern seriously while preserving evidence status. It connects digital and offline circumstances, avoids blame and diagnostic shortcuts, and uses no sensitive images or credentials.

modules.title: Safe contact and specialist planning
modules.outcome: Prepare a person-led support outline before suggesting technical or reporting changes.
paragraphs: A communication route that is convenient for the worker may be unsafe or inaccessible for the person seeking support. Before an actual contact, authorised staff need to agree appropriate channel, timing, message content and what to do if contact is interrupted. Do not assume an email address is private, that a shared phone is independently controlled or that a missed message means consent to another method. In the fictional exercise, identify these planning questions without sending test messages, contacting a real account or placing sensitive information in a calendar or class submission. [S18, S17, S1]

Changing access can alter what another person notices. Removing a device, changing credentials, deleting content or making a platform report may affect safety, evidence or continued access to work and support. There is no universal action sequence suitable for every situation. The NNEDV guide is a specialist planning comparator with 2018 US context, not a current Nigerian technical or legal protocol. Use its planning principle to explain why qualified advice and the person's priorities should precede a proposed change; do not reproduce a device checklist or present old symptom examples as reliable surveillance tests. [S18, S1]

An introductory worker can acknowledge the concern, clarify role and service limits and facilitate appropriate specialist options through approved arrangements. The worker should not demand passwords, log in to an account, install a monitoring app, bypass access controls or direct a confrontation. A qualified technology-abuse specialist may be needed alongside GBV, legal or clinical support, depending on the person's needs. Verify the actual service's scope and safe contact conditions rather than promise that a platform, police unit or advocate will remove content, accept a case or achieve a particular outcome. [S17, S18]

A bounded support outline records only necessary planning information within authorised systems and explains confidentiality limits appropriately. It should identify who can take the next step, what remains undecided and how the person can revisit preferences. Avoid promising that private browsing, a VPN or any single setting guarantees safety. Technology changes and local processes require current specialist knowledge. A course completion badge demonstrates completion under the academy's approved assessment requirements; it does not grant authority for forensic work, independent safeguarding decisions or unsupervised technical intervention on someone else's device. [S18, S17, S1]
modules.example: Fictional case: a support worker plans to email an adult about a digital-abuse referral, but the adult has not agreed that email is private. The learner pauses the proposed contact and identifies safe-contact and specialist-planning questions without testing the account.
modules.activity: Prepare a conditional next-step note with preferred contact questions, two possible consequences of unplanned account changes, role limits, a qualified referral dependency and a way to revisit preferences.
modules.feedback: A sound outline avoids assuming channel safety and does not prescribe blanket resets or reporting. It connects person-led priorities with current specialist advice and makes the next action conditional on appropriate arrangements.

modules.title: Reporting information and accountable follow-up
modules.outcome: Distinguish survivor choice, technical evidence handling and programme claims without exposing material.
paragraphs: Platform reporting, legal processes and specialist evidence handling are different activities. A report button does not guarantee removal, confidentiality, protection or preservation of information. Requirements vary by service, platform, jurisdiction and circumstance. A learner should explain the need for qualified current advice without promising an outcome or giving a universal instruction to save or delete material. Do not ask a person to forward intimate images, access an abusive actor's account or gather evidence through confrontation. Actual urgent safeguarding concerns should follow authorised procedures, not a classroom decision tree. [S17, S18, S1]

Consent to one support purpose does not authorise copying a person's account into a presentation, a training database or a public advocacy story. Removing names may not protect identity if a screenshot, location, role or combination of details remains recognisable. Course submissions use only fictional descriptions, with no personal records. An authorised service should use its approved information-handling procedures and explain relevant limits honestly. The worker's desire to demonstrate helpfulness, document an impressive case or obtain a platform response does not override purpose limitation, confidentiality or the person's informed choices. [S1, S17]

Measures of technology-facilitated sexual violence vary in what they include and whose experiences they reflect. The 2026 measurement scoping review catalogues measures but does not appraise study quality or establish their robustness. Its coverage is heavily Western high-income, and its focus is narrower than all GBV. Counting reports, removed posts or accounts changed cannot by itself demonstrate that harm ended or that a support programme caused improvement. A local evaluation would need a relevant construct, suitable methods, ethical arrangements and appropriate validation rather than a copied questionnaire selected because it appears in a review. [R28, R27]

Follow-up should be feasible, agreed and limited to the appropriate role. A fictional note can identify the person-led goal, the dependency on a qualified service, the agreed contact question and a point to revisit unresolved needs. A completed referral offer differs from assistance accessed, and removal of one item differs from sustained safety or recovery. Do not blame the person if a platform action fails or preferences change. Keep uncertainty and service constraints visible, seek supervision when a concern exceeds scope and review whether the process itself introduced burdens or unwanted exposure. [S18, S17, S1]
modules.example: Fictional case: a project counts platform reports as successful recovery and wants to use a private account story in a promotional slide. A learner separates the output from the unsupported outcome and rejects reusing the account without an appropriate purpose and permissions.
modules.activity: Write a follow-up and reporting critique: output observed, outcome not established, privacy concern, specialist dependency and agreed review question. Use no platform account, image or real incident data.
modules.feedback: A careful critique distinguishes platform actions from safety outcomes, uses the measurement evidence within its limits and keeps support information out of unapproved secondary uses.

questions.question: A learner offers a private intimate screenshot as evidence for the digital-safety worksheet. What fits the exercise?

questions.question: A fictional adult has not agreed that email is private. What should precede a sensitive referral message?

options.text: Send the full history because email is fast.
Assume an address proves sole account control.
Try several contact methods until someone answers.
Appropriate agreement on channel, timing and content through authorised arrangements.

questions.question: A learner proposes immediately deleting an account after a reported threat. What is the appropriate planning correction?

options.text: Consider the person's priorities and possible safety, evidence and access effects with qualified advice.
Deletion always has no consequences.
An account reset is universally safe.
The learner's preference replaces the person's needs.

questions.question: The NNEDV page carries a 2018 copyright and US examples. How should it be used here?

options.text: As a 2026 Nigerian reporting law.
As a bounded planning comparator with current local specialist advice still needed.
As a guaranteed diagnosis from a single device symptom.
As proof that every listed service operates locally.

questions.question: A learner offers to collect a person's password to investigate a fictional concern. Which boundary applies?

options.text: Store the password in the worksheet for convenience.
Share the account with classmates to check it.
Do not collect credentials or access accounts; identify appropriate specialist support.
Install monitoring software as a course exercise.

questions.rationale: Introductory support is not account access or technical investigation.

questions.question: A fictional plan says private browsing guarantees that an abusive actor cannot learn about help-seeking. What correction is needed?

options.text: Keep the claim because one feature solves all risks.
Assume every device is independently controlled.
Replace discussion of priorities with a universal app recommendation.
Remove the guarantee and consider the actual context with qualified safety planning.

questions.rationale: A feature-specific assertion cannot establish overall safety.

questions.question: A fictional support note promises that using a report button will remove all risk. What is defensible instead?

options.text: Explain uncertain outcomes and seek appropriate current specialist advice within the person's priorities.
Treat submission of a report as guaranteed recovery.
Promise that every platform preserves evidence identically.
Assume reporting cannot affect safety or access.

questions.rationale: Platform actions and personal safety are distinct and context-dependent.

questions.question: A service wants to turn a private digital-abuse account into course promotion. What remains necessary?

options.text: Permission inferred from accepting support.
Appropriate separate purpose, permissions and risk review; the support purpose alone is insufficient.
Automatic reuse if names are removed.
A claim that publicity is always in the person's interests.

questions.rationale: Information gathered for support is not automatically available for secondary use.

questions.question: A planner selects a questionnaire solely because the JMIR scoping review lists it. What is missing?

options.text: Proof that every listed tool is Nigerian-validated.
A conclusion that scoping reviews certify all instruments.
Appraisal of construct, validation, context, permissions and ethical suitability.
Permission to copy every questionnaire item.

questions.rationale: The review maps measures without quality appraisal or universal validation.

questions.question: One reported post is removed. Which follow-up claim is appropriately limited?

options.text: All offline and online harm necessarily ended.
The platform action proves clinical recovery.
No further person-led review can be relevant.
The item was removed; wider needs and agreed goals require separate review.

questions.rationale: A specific action does not establish every broader outcome.

questions.question: A fictional adult no longer wants the initially discussed platform action. What should a support outline allow?

options.text: Revisiting preferences and appropriate options through agreed safe contact and qualified support.
Continuing solely because the worker already wrote the plan.
Treating a changed preference as failure by the person.
Publishing the account to pressure agreement.

questions.rationale: Person-led support recognises changing choices and circumstances.

courses.title: Ethical GBV Data and Programme Evaluation
courses.cover_title:
Ethical GBV Data
and Programme Evaluation
courses.school_name: School of Gender Studies and Gender-Based Violence Prevention
courses.audience: Introductory social work and community-service learners using non-graphic fictional scenarios. No specialist child/GBV casework, clinical, forensic, legal or research competence is conferred; supervised skills and safeguarding review are separate requirements.
courses.study_guidance: Use only the supplied non-graphic fictional scenarios and aggregate exercise data. Do not seek real disclosures, investigate allegations or submit survivor records, passwords or images. Write your reasoning before checking feedback. You may pause or use an alternative fictional exercise; supervised skills review remains separate.
courses.practice_safety_note: Use only the supplied non-graphic fictional scenario or aggregate exercise data. Do not collect real disclosures or submit survivor records, passwords or images. You may pause or use an alternative fictional exercise. Record reasoning before checking guide feedback.
courses.outcome: Critique a fictional GBV data and evaluation proposal through purpose limitation, confidentiality, defined measures and appropriately bounded conclusions, without collecting real survivor information.

modules.title: Purpose consent and the information lifecycle
modules.outcome: Distinguish information purposes and specify a minimum-data governance outline.
paragraphs: Begin with the decision or service purpose, not a list of information that might someday be useful. Sensitive data create responsibilities at collection, recording, access, storage, analysis, sharing, retention and disposal. Ask who needs each field for the stated purpose and whether a less identifying alternative would suffice. The October 2026 UNFPA guidance addresses GBV service data in integrated programming; it does not authorise learners to conduct research or obtain case files. This course uses fictional aggregate exercise data only and never requires incident narratives, contact details or actual service records. [S19, S1]

Health records and GBV case-management information serve distinct functions and operate under different professional arrangements. Co-location, coordination or a shared funding source does not automatically authorise combining them. A provider's legitimate need for a specific referral detail is not permission to receive an entire case file. Actual systems need approved governance, purpose-specific access and appropriate agreements, with qualified roles handling clinical, safeguarding and legal questions. In a fictional analysis, name the separate purposes and identify the authority that must resolve a sharing request rather than design an unrestricted shared spreadsheet. [S19, S10]

Informed consent concerns a specific understood purpose and relevant choices, benefits, risks and limits. Consent to receive help is not automatic consent to research, publicity or cross-service analysis. Do not promise confidentiality without exceptions or invent a universal rule for reporting or emergency disclosure. Applicable law, organisational safeguarding procedures, the person's circumstances and qualified decisions matter, particularly for children. A learner can identify where expert review is required; the worksheet does not grant permission to collect information or decide a real exception because the proposed use seems beneficial. [S19, S1]

Privacy risks can remain after names are removed. A combination of location, timing, role or a rare circumstance may identify someone, and even an aggregate figure may be sensitive in context. Limit access and outputs to the approved purpose, assess indirect identification and use the organisation's authorised security and retention arrangements. A fictional governance note should state responsible roles, an access boundary, a retention decision requiring approval and a process for concerns or incidents. It should not specify a universal retention period, certify legal compliance or treat a password alone as a complete information-protection system. [S19, S20, S10]
modules.example: Fictional case: a co-located clinic and GBV service propose combining all records for a sponsor dashboard. A learner distinguishes clinical and case-management purposes, asks what the dashboard decision needs and identifies a qualified governance review before any sharing.
modules.activity: Write a minimum-data governance note with purpose, unnecessary fields, distinct record types, consent limits, indirect-identification concern, responsible authority and an unresolved retention question. Use no real records.
modules.feedback: A defensible note begins with purpose, separates clinical and casework information and avoids assuming coordination permits unrestricted linkage. Consent and confidentiality limits require appropriate qualified decisions.

modules.title: Counts denominators and service indicators
modules.outcome: Calculate fictional proportions and state what service data can and cannot establish.
paragraphs: An indicator needs an explicit definition: what is counted, the unit, the period, the eligible group, the source and how missing information is handled. Visits, referrals offered, referrals accepted and unique people are different units. A person may use a service more than once or appear in more than one provider's figures. An apparently simple total can therefore double-count, omit groups or conceal uncertainty. Do not remove those uncertainties by quietly assuming every record is a different person or that every offer resulted in support accessed. [S20, S19]

Consider an invented exercise in which completed referrals are twelve of thirty eligible referrals in one period and eighteen of sixty in another. The corresponding proportions are forty percent and thirty percent. The completed count increased while the proportion decreased by ten percentage points. State both numerator and denominator and do not call that a ten percent relative decrease. Comparability still depends on definitions, periods and the eligible groups. These fictional aggregates are for arithmetic and interpretation; they are not real service performance, evidence of violence change or a target for judging individual staff. [S20, S19]

Service data concern people who reached particular services under particular recording conditions. They are not population prevalence data. Higher recorded use may reflect improved access, changing capacity, altered definitions, repeated contacts or other factors, and cannot by itself establish that violence increased. Lower use may reflect barriers rather than reduced need. The 2026 guidance explicitly distinguishes service information from prevalence research. A learner should state that limit clearly rather than divide a service total by a convenient community population and label the result the local rate of GBV. [S19, S10]

Missing information is an evidence limitation, not a zero. If follow-up is unavailable, a referral outcome is unknown rather than automatically completed or failed. Explain coverage without attempting to fill gaps through unapproved survivor contact, record linkage or investigation. Any real analytic request needs qualified data governance, purpose-specific permissions and appropriate safety review. A fictional indicator note should show the calculation, denominator, relevant uncertainty and a bounded review question, with only the minimum approved reporting detail. Clean-looking tables do not compensate for an unsuitable measure or unsafe information process. [S20, S19, S1]
modules.example: Fictional dataset: period A has twelve completed referrals among thirty eligible referrals; period B has eighteen among sixty. No individual records are supplied. A draft report says the completion rate rose because eighteen exceeds twelve.
modules.activity: Calculate both proportions and their percentage-point difference. Correct the report, identify two comparability questions, distinguish unknown follow-up from zero and explain why these figures cannot estimate GBV prevalence.
modules.feedback: A is 40% and B is 30%, a decrease of 10 percentage points despite a higher completed count. Definitions, coverage and period comparability remain to check. Service referrals do not measure population prevalence or causal programme impact.

modules.title: Evaluation design feedback and bounded conclusions
modules.outcome: Match a review question to appropriate evidence and an accountable response.
paragraphs: Monitoring describes delivery and relevant changes over time; evaluation asks structured questions about a programme's design, implementation or results. Begin with a question that can be answered safely within the available authority and resources. A service-access review is different from a study of violence reduction, and both differ from an individual clinical assessment. For coursework, critique a fictional proposal rather than recruit participants, administer a sensitive instrument or request private files. Actual GBV research and consultation require qualified ethical, safeguarding, methodological and service arrangements beyond an introductory course. [S20, S10, S1]

A measure should match the construct and population. A questionnaire focused on technology-facilitated sexual violence cannot automatically represent every form of GBV or all aspects of service quality. The 2026 measurement review maps 218 measures across 319 studies but does not appraise study quality or establish robustness. Its heavily Western high-income coverage limits transfer. Selection for an actual study would require appropriate validation, cultural and language suitability, ethical review and permissions; appearing in an open-access review does not license copying an instrument or prove that it is suitable for Nigeria. [R28, S1]

Interpret findings in line with the design. A before/after difference without an appropriate comparison may reflect changing groups, reporting, service capacity or wider conditions. A satisfaction response is one perspective, not proof of recovery or absence of violence. Missing perspectives and feedback conditions matter: pressure to praise a provider can distort a review, while a small-group summary may expose identity. Do not treat a larger number of records as a substitute for safe collection and relevant evidence. Report the question, source, coverage, method and limitations so an authorised reader can assess the actual claim. [S20, S19, R28]

An evaluation is useful when it informs a proportionate decision and an accountable response. State what should change, who can authorise it, a resource dependency and a point to review the response. If evidence is insufficient, say what remains unknown rather than claim success or failure beyond the measure. Feedback should be offered through appropriate safe routes and should not be linked to continued access to support. This course develops critical interpretation using fictional material; it does not authorise real GBV data collection, approve a research protocol or replace independent curriculum and supervised skills review. [S10, S20, S1]
modules.example: Fictional case: a service claims recovery from a higher referral count and proposes copying a foreign digital-abuse questionnaire into an unapproved survey. A learner separates the claims, identifies measure and ethical-review gaps and recommends a bounded authorised service-access review.
modules.activity: Write an evaluation brief with question, appropriate evidence type, unsuitable inference, measure-transfer concern, missing-perspective check and an action owner. State what requires qualified approval before real collection.
modules.feedback: A defensible brief matches evidence to the question, recognises validation and design limits and avoids unapproved collection or copied instruments. Its recommendation identifies authority and follow-through without claiming causal recovery.

assessment.title: Ethical GBV Data and Programme Evaluation

modules.title: Purpose consent and the information lifecycle
modules.outcome: Distinguish information purposes and specify a minimum-data governance outline.

teaching_points.text: Data collection should follow a justified purpose.
Clinical and GBV case records have distinct functions.
Service consent does not automatically permit research.
Removing names does not guarantee anonymity.
Legal and safeguarding exceptions require qualified handling.

modules.title: Counts denominators and service indicators
modules.outcome: Calculate fictional proportions and state what service data can and cannot establish.

teaching_points.text: Counts and proportions can move in different directions.
Percentage points differ from relative percent change.
Service use is not population prevalence.
Unknown follow-up is not zero or confirmed success.
Comparable indicators need defined units and eligibility.

modules.title: Evaluation design feedback and bounded conclusions
modules.outcome: Match a review question to appropriate evidence and an accountable response.

teaching_points.text: The review question determines the evidence needed.
An open-access article does not validate or license every instrument it lists.
A before/after service change has alternative explanations.
Feedback conditions affect interpretation.
Evaluation findings should lead to proportionate accountable action.

questions.question: A fictional dashboard requests every available field for possible future use. What is the first correction?

options.text: Copy all records before deciding what is useful.
Assume more identifying detail always improves safety.
Define the decision and collect only information justified for that purpose.
Treat sponsor interest as complete data-collection authority.

questions.rationale: Purpose and minimisation should precede information gathering.

questions.question: A clinic and a GBV service share a building. What does this alone authorise?

options.text: Unrestricted access to all clinical and case notes.
A public combined survivor spreadsheet.
Research use without separate governance.
No automatic sharing or linkage of their full records.

questions.rationale: Co-location does not remove professional purpose, access and consent boundaries.

questions.question: A fictional client agrees to a support referral. What should not be inferred?

options.text: Permission for unrelated research, promotion or unrestricted secondary analysis.
That the referral purpose has limits.
That confidentiality needs an appropriate explanation.
That only necessary information should be considered.

questions.rationale: A specific service choice cannot supply blanket consent for other uses.

questions.question: A table omits names but identifies a unique role and small location. What remains necessary?

options.text: Declare it anonymous solely because the name column is gone.
Assess contextual identification and reporting risks before approved sharing.
Publish it automatically as aggregate data.
Assume every indirect identifier is harmless.

questions.rationale: Combinations of details may remain identifying.

questions.question: A learner wants to decide a real reporting exception using the course worksheet. What boundary applies?

options.text: Any beneficial purpose overrides all privacy limits.
One universal rule covers every jurisdiction and child.
Use designated qualified procedures and context-specific advice; the worksheet is not authorisation.
A high quiz score creates legal decision authority.

questions.rationale: The course identifies governance questions rather than deciding actual exceptions.

questions.question: Completed referrals change from twelve of thirty to eighteen of sixty in a fictional exercise. What are the proportions?

options.text: Thirty percent followed by forty percent.
Twelve percent followed by eighteen percent.
Both are sixty percent because the second count is larger.
Forty percent followed by thirty percent.

questions.question: A fictional completion proportion changes from 40% to 30%. What is the absolute percentage-point change?

options.text: A decrease of ten percentage points.
An increase of ten percentage points.
A decrease of ten percent relative to the original rate.
No change because both figures are percentages.

questions.rationale: Subtracting proportions gives ten percentage points; relative change is a different calculation.

questions.question: Recorded GBV service visits rise in one month. What can be concluded from that count alone?

options.text: Violence prevalence necessarily rose by the same amount.
Recorded visits rose; population violence prevalence and the cause of the change remain unestablished.
Every visit represents a different person.
The programme necessarily caused increased violence.

questions.rationale: Use depends on access, definitions, repeat contacts and other conditions.

questions.question: A fictional referral record has no follow-up outcome. How should it be represented in a review?

options.text: Automatically as successful completion.
Automatically as a failure caused by the learner.
As unknown under a defined missing-data rule, with coverage stated.
As permission to contact the person through any available channel.

questions.rationale: Missing evidence should remain visible without unsafe gap-filling.

questions.question: Two services report twenty contacts and twenty unique clients. What should an analyst avoid?

options.text: Stating the reporting period.
Clarifying eligible groups.
Explaining a possible double-counting limitation.
Treating the units as interchangeable without checking definitions and repeat use.

questions.rationale: Contacts and distinct people are different analytic units.

questions.question: A fictional team wants to assess service access but proposes an unrelated violence-prevalence claim. What should be clarified first?

options.text: The actual question, relevant construct, ethical scope and feasible method.
Which unrelated headline will attract most attention.
How to collect the maximum private detail.
How to label all monitoring as a clinical assessment.

questions.rationale: Different questions require different evidence and safeguards.

questions.question: A listed foreign questionnaire is proposed for a Nigerian GBV survey. What must be considered before actual use?

options.text: Only the journal logo.
Construct fit, local validation, permissions and qualified ethical and safeguarding review.
Automatic validity because the review is recent.
An assumption that all listed instruments are unrestricted.

questions.rationale: Evidence mapping, validation and instrument rights are separate questions.

questions.question: A fictional service records more referrals after a campaign. What limits a causal-effect claim?

options.text: The calendar sequence alone proves causation.
More records guarantee less violence.
Changes in access, recording, groups or wider conditions may also explain the observation.
An attractive chart removes confounding.

questions.rationale: An uncontrolled observation cannot identify the programme as the sole cause.

questions.question: People are told that positive feedback helps them retain support. What is wrong with the proposed review?

options.text: It guarantees unbiased satisfaction data.
It makes confidentiality unnecessary.
It proves every respondent recovered.
The pressure undermines voluntary feedback and may distort findings.

questions.rationale: Feedback should not be coerced or linked to continued assistance.

questions.question: A fictional review identifies an unresolved access barrier. Which recommendation is useful?

options.text: An authorised owner, feasible corrective action, resource condition and review point with limits stated.
A universal success claim without evidence.
Publishing case details to create pressure.
Collecting more sensitive records without approval.

questions.rationale: Accountability connects a supported finding to an appropriate response.

evidence_note: Checked 15 November 2026. Publication dates and evidence periods are distinguished. Current 2025/2026 guidance and OA research are appraised alongside older specialist resources. Provider-indexed SJR and publisher-reported JIF Q1 status are identified with access limits; no BMJ Public Health, IJGO or IJSDS quartile is asserted. Journal rank is not article validity. Independent GBV/safeguarding, Nigerian practice/legal, accessibility, pilot and supervised skills reviews remain pending.
